GENERAL.healthInsuranceDescriptionLong: Health insurance is a critical financial tool designed to cover medical and surgical costs. Depending on the type of health insurance plan, either the insured pays out-of-pocket and is later reimbursed, or the insurer makes direct payments to the provider. Health insurance policies typically cover doctor visits, hospital stays, preventive care, and prescription medications. Some plans may also offer coverage for mental health services, vision care, and dental care. Having health insurance is essential because it helps mitigate the high costs associated with healthcare, providing individuals and families with the necessary medical care without excessive financial burden.
GENERAL.lifeInsuranceDescriptionLong: Life insurance is an agreement between an individual and an insurance company, in which the insurer agrees to pay a designated beneficiary a specified sum of money upon the death of the insured person. This type of insurance provides financial protection and peace of mind by ensuring that loved ones are financially secured after the insured's death. Life insurance can cover various expenses, including funeral costs, outstanding debts, mortgage repayments, and daily living expenses. Some policies also offer living benefits, which may be available under certain conditions, providing additional financial support during the insured's lifetime.
GENERAL.carInsuranceDescriptionLong: Car insurance is a policy purchased by vehicle owners to minimize the costs associated with being involved in a car accident or vehicle damage. It covers various events such as collisions, theft, vandalism, and damages caused by natural disasters. Car insurance typically includes liability coverage, which covers damages or injuries you cause to others, and may also offer comprehensive and collision coverage for your own vehicle. Additionally, policies may cover medical payments, personal injury protection, and coverage against uninsured/underinsured drivers. Having car insurance is essential for financial protection and legal compliance, ensuring that drivers can cover unexpected expenses related to their vehicles.
GENERAL.houseInsuranceDescriptionLong: Home insurance, also known as homeowners insurance, provides financial protection against damage to your home and personal belongings as a result of covered events such as fire, theft, vandalism, and natural disasters. It also offers liability coverage in case someone is injured on your property or you cause damage to someone else's property. Home insurance policies typically cover the structure of the house, personal property, additional living expenses if you need to temporarily relocate, and liability. Having home insurance is crucial for protecting one of your biggest investments and ensuring financial stability in the event of unforeseen circumstances.
GENERAL.lawProtectionDescriptionLong: Legal protection insurance, also known as legal expenses insurance, covers the costs associated with legal expenses incurred by the insured in the event of legal disputes. This type of insurance can help cover attorney fees, court costs, and other legal expenses in various situations such as employment disputes, contractual issues, personal injury claims, and family matters. Legal protection insurance provides access to legal advice and representation, reducing the financial burden associated with legal proceedings and ensuring that individuals can seek justice and protect their rights without worrying about high costs.
GENERAL.petInsuranceDescriptionLong: Pet insurance helps cover the costs of veterinary care for your pets, ensuring they receive necessary treatment without causing financial strain. This type of insurance typically covers accidents, illnesses, surgeries, and routine care such as vaccinations and preventive treatments. Some policies may also offer coverage for hereditary and congenital conditions, dental care, and alternative therapies. Pet insurance allows pet owners to focus on the health and well-being of their furry friends rather than on the expenses associated with veterinary visits, providing peace of mind and financial support when their pets need it the most.

CAR.title: Car Insurance
CAR.infoList: In Switzerland, we distinguish two types of car insurance:

intro.title: Basic Insurance
intro.p:
Basic health insurance in Switzerland, called 'Grundversicherung', is mandatory for everyone living in the country. It must be purchased within 90 days of starting work in Switzerland. It covers essential medical services such as doctor visits, hospital treatment in general wards, prescription medications, and emergency care. Everyone can choose their own insurer from many companies that offer the same legally defined services.
Basic insurance can be changed each year until the end of November.

OC.title: Liability Insurance
OC.p:
In Switzerland, this is a mandatory insurance for owners of motor vehicles, such as cars and motorcycles. It is required by law and is a prerequisite for registering a vehicle and obtaining license plates.​
Having this insurance provides financial protection in case of third-party claims arising from road accidents. Not having a valid policy makes it illegal to drive on Swiss roads and may lead to serious legal consequences.

Examples:
OC.i1: While parking, the driver damages a vehicle behind them.
OC.i2: Due to sunlight, the driver fails to notice a pedestrian at a crosswalk and hits them.
OC.i3: Oil leaks from a parked car. A motorcyclist slips on the oil and is seriously injured; the motorcycle is totally destroyed.
OC.i4: When getting out of a parked car, the driver fails to see an approaching cyclist. The cyclist cannot avoid the door and falls heavily.

casco.title: Casco Insurance
casco.p: This is a voluntary but very popular type of car insurance that provides broad protection for vehicle owners against financial consequences resulting from damage, destruction, or loss of the vehicle. It covers damages not caused by other road users, offering protection not only in case of collisions but also in situations caused by natural events or random incidents. Casco insurance provides peace of mind due to its wide coverage, especially valuable for owners of expensive or new cars exposed to risks such as theft, weather damage, or accidents beyond the owner's control.
casco.p2: There are two types of Casco insurance:

teilkasko.title: Partial Casco (Teilkasko)
teilkasko.p: Covers damages not caused by the driver's fault, such as:
teilkasko.i7: vandalism (e.g. broken antennas, mirrors, punctured tires)

vollkasko.title: Full Casco (Vollkasko)
vollkasko.p: Includes all Partial Casco benefits and additionally:
vollkasko.li1: damages caused by the driver (e.g. collisions with other vehicles or objects),

kask.li2: Teilkasko: Recommended for mid-value vehicles, typically up to 7 years old.
kask.li3: Vollkasko: Especially recommended for new or leased vehicles, where financial risk is higher.

OC.title: Personal Liability Insurance
OC.info: Personal liability insurance is optional coverage that protects you financially if you accidentally cause harm to another person—either through injury or property damage. It’s one of the most important types of insurance for renters, pet owners, and individuals in general. While it’s not legally required, it can save you from significant compensation costs, such as flooding a neighbor’s apartment, injuring a cyclist, or damage caused by your child or pet.

what.title: What the insurance covers
what.il1: Injury caused to a third party – e.g., you accidentally hit a cyclist while riding an e-scooter
what.il2: Damage to someone else’s property – e.g., you break someone’s phone or flood your neighbor’s flat
what.il3: Damage caused by your underage child
what.il4: Damage caused by your dog (if you have one)
what.il5: Damage caused by you as a tenant – e.g., you damage the wall or floor in a rented apartment

example.title: Examples of covered incidents
example.il1: Your friend accidentally spills a glass of red wine on your dress. The stain can’t be removed.
example.i1: Personal liability insurance covers the damage.
example.il2: A child playing with a ball breaks a neighbor’s window by accident.
example.il3: Matches left within reach of a child cause a fire that spreads to a neighbor’s shed, damaging it.
example.il4: You let your dog off the leash during a walk. Feeling threatened, it bites a boy playing football.
example.il5: In your rented flat, a heavy object falls into the sink and breaks it.
example.il6: A step at the entrance to your home is damaged. A guest slips on it and gets injured. You’re liable for the damage.

HEALTH.title: Health Insurance
HEALTH.info: The health insurance system in Switzerland stands out from those in other countries. Every person residing in Switzerland is required to choose their own insurer and pay health insurance premiums regularly. Unlike in most European countries and many others around the world, these premiums are not automatically deducted from wages.
HEALTH.infoList: There are two types of insurance:

basic.title: Basic Insurance
basic.p:
The basic health insurance in Switzerland, called 'Grundversicherung', is mandatory for everyone residing in the country. It must be purchased within 90 days of starting work in Switzerland. It covers essential medical services, such as doctor visits, hospital treatment in a general ward, prescription medications, and emergency care. Everyone can choose their insurer from many available companies that offer the same services as defined by law.
The basic insurance can be changed annually until the end of November.
basic.p1: Factors that affect the cost of basic insurance

fran.title: Deductible
fran.p:
This is the amount you must pay out-of-pocket for medical services during the year before the insurer starts covering the treatment costs.
Keep in mind that the lower the deductible, the higher the monthly premium, and the higher the deductible, the lower the costs.
fran.p1: The following deductible levels are available
fran.p7: Once the deductible has been reached, we must cover 10% of the remaining costs, but no more than CHF 700 for adults or CHF 350 for children. Beyond this limit, all costs are covered by the insurer.
fran.p9:
After a 5-day hospital stay, we receive a bill of CHF 10,000.
We assume our deductible is CHF 300.
fran.p10: First, we must pay the amount of our deductible, which is CHF 300.
fran.p11:
Next, 10% of the remaining amount.
The remaining amount is CHF 10,000 – CHF 300 = CHF 9,700.
fran.p12:
10% of CHF 9,700 is CHF 970
(remember that the maximum amount from the remaining 10% is CHF 700)
so CHF 970 becomes CHF 700.
fran.p13:
Add CHF 300 + CHF 700 = CHF 1,000 .
This is the amount we will have to pay out of pocket.

model.title: Insurance Model
model.p:
The insurance model refers to the way you access medical services under your health insurance. In Switzerland, different models are available that affect the premium amount as well as the organization of healthcare services.
In cases of emergencies, vision problems, or annual gynecological check-ups, the choice of model does not matter.
model.p2:
Traditional
You can freely choose your primary care physician and specialists (without a referral from a family doctor). It is the most expensive but offers the greatest flexibility.
model.p3:
HMO (Health Maintenance Organization)
Treatment is provided within a network of designated doctors (clinics) and hospitals. Premiums are lower, but the choice of doctors is limited.
model.p4:
Telmed
You first contact a telephone center, which directs you to the appropriate doctor.
model.p5:
Family doctor model
You always first visit your primary care physician, who coordinates further treatment. You must choose your doctor from a list of available specialists when signing up for the policy.

add.title: Supplementary Insurance
add.p: This is voluntary health insurance that expands the range of services offered by the basic insurance. It allows you to access additional benefits, such as:
add.i2: treatment in private hospitals or clinics,
add.i5: reimbursement for the purchase of glasses, gym memberships.
add.p2:
Opting for supplementary insurance provides greater freedom in choosing doctors, hospitals, and treatment methods, as well as better treatment conditions. Although it comes with higher premiums, the investment in supplementary insurance offers more comprehensive health protection and comfort when needed, helping to avoid high costs for medical services that are not covered by basic insurance.
Supplementary insurance can usually be changed every 3 years, until the end of September.

extra.title: More About Basic Insurance
extra.i1: Basic insurance must cover the costs of medications that are on the list approved by specialists and prescribed by a doctor. This list, which includes around 2,500 medications, is regularly updated.
extra.i2: In cases of medical transport that does not involve an immediate life-threatening situation, basic insurance covers 50% of the costs, but no more than CHF 500 per year. Transports related to emergencies and hospital transfers are fully reimbursed.
extra.i3: Basic insurance only covers essential treatment in emergency cases abroad, up to a maximum of twice the cost of the same treatment in Switzerland. For travel outside the EU/EFTA, it is recommended to purchase additional insurance.
extra.i4: Basic insurance in Switzerland covers dental treatment only to a limited extent. Usually, only urgent cases are reimbursed, such as treatment following accidents (e.g., broken teeth) or treatment related to oral diseases that may affect overall health.
extra.i5: Basic insurance covers gynecological examinations and Pap smears every three years, and if necessary, also annually (after consultation with the insurer).
extra.i6: Basic health insurance covers the costs of services before and after childbirth. These include:
extra.il1: Seven routine examinations (including two ultrasounds: one between the 11th and 14th week of pregnancy and one between the 20th and 23rd week). In high-risk pregnancies, additional ultrasounds may be conducted at the doctor's request.
extra.il2: Preparation for childbirth and perinatal care provided by doctors or midwives – basic insurance covers a cost of CHF 150.
extra.il3: From the 12th week of pregnancy, a non-invasive prenatal test is performed.
extra.il4: Costs of home birth or birth in a general ward of a hospital in the canton of residence.
extra.il5: Postpartum check-up between the 6th and 10th week, and up to three lactation consultations.
extra.p7: It is important to note that services related to pregnancy and childbirth do not involve any co-payments or deductibles. In cases of health complications for the woman, from the 13th week of pregnancy until 8 weeks postpartum, no additional costs are incurred.
extra.i8: Basic insurance may cover the costs of psychological therapy, but under certain conditions. Since 1 July 2022, basic insurance covers psychological therapy provided by qualified psychotherapists, provided that the therapy is prescribed by a doctor. This means that an initial consultation with a doctor, who will provide a referral, is required.
extra.i9: Costs may be reimbursed according to the standard terms of the insurance, which include the deductible and co-payment (max CHF 700). Therapies conducted privately, without a doctor's referral, are generally not covered by basic insurance and require the purchase of supplementary health insurance.
extra.i10: The hospital must be on the list approved by the canton. If it is not on the list, you must cover the difference in treatment costs between hospitals (to avoid these costs, supplementary insurance should be purchased).
extra.i11: A fee of CHF 15 is required for each day of hospitalization (regardless of the type of insurance).
extra.i12: Costs for stays in private or semi-private facilities require supplementary insurance

newcommers.p:
Remember, you have 90 days from the start of your employment to get insurance. If you don't, a penalty will be applied.
Bills will need to be paid retroactively - exactly from the first day of registration.
newcommers.p2: Documents you need to get insurance:
newcommers.p3: This is the registration confirmation with the start date of employment and your address. To obtain this document, you need to go to the local municipality (Gemeinde) with:
newcommers.p4: To open a bank account, you need an employment contract and a residence permit (Bewiligung). The process of getting the residence permit (Swiss ID) can take several weeks, and the whole insurance process can take significantly longer. The solution is to open an account with PostFinance bank. In this case, you only need an ID, employment contract, and registration confirmation (Meldebestätigung).

LAW.title: Legal protection
LAW.info:
This is a voluntary insurance that protects against costs related to legal proceedings. In case of legal conflicts, such as disputes with an employer, landlord, or after road accidents, this insurance covers, among others, lawyer fees, court costs, and possible compensation for the opposing party. It also provides support in the form of legal advice and, if necessary, legal representation.

Having this insurance can provide peace of mind, knowing that in case of legal issues, you won't be left alone with high costs and complex procedures.

The insurance has a three-month waiting period.

costs.title: What costs are covered by the insurance?
costs.il5: Court fees and other procedural costs
costs.il7: Advance payment of the amount determined by the court
costs.il8: Debt collection costs for claims the insured can pursue after the process

priv.title: Which legal areas are covered by private legal protection insurance?

HOUSE.title: Home Insurance
HOUSE.info: This is a voluntary household contents insurance in Switzerland that protects against financial losses caused by events such as fire, flooding, theft, or damage caused by natural forces. It covers everyday items like furniture, electronics, clothing, or bicycles. In the event of damage, the insurer covers the cost of repair or replacement. Although not mandatory, having Hausratversicherung is highly recommended to protect against unexpected expenses.

what.title: What is insured?
what.il1: All items not permanently attached to the building/property
what.il3: Items used for business purposes are not insured

additional.title: What can be additionally insured?
additional.il4: Theft of mopeds and e-bikes with license plates

important.title: Important information!
important.li1: Deductible for all insured risks is CHF 200.
important.li2: Deductible for natural damage is CHF 500.

casco.title: Casco Insurance (Household – KASKO)
casco.p: This insurance covers damages caused directly by the owner. It reimburses the purchase of a new item of equivalent value (minus the deductible).

clientStories.title: Real Client Outcomes
clientStories.lead: A few practical examples of how the right supplementary coverage can reduce yearly out-of-pocket costs.

cases.name: Monika, 43
cases.body: Monika had been visiting a recognised acupuncturist and TCM therapist for several years, spending around CHF 1,400 annually. Her previous supplementary insurance provided only limited reimbursement. After reviewing her needs, she switched to Helsana COMPLETA, which reimburses 75% of eligible complementary medicine treatments provided by recognised practitioners. Her supplementary premium increased by CHF 18 per month (CHF 216 per year). With approximately CHF 1,050 reimbursed, she continued the same treatments while substantially reducing her annual healthcare costs.

cases.name: Daniel, 36
cases.body: Daniel wears contact lenses during the week and replaces his prescription glasses every few years. His annual optical expenses average CHF 900. After switching to Helsana COMPLETA, he became eligible for 90% reimbursement on spectacle lenses and contact lenses, up to CHF 300 per calendar year. His supplementary premium increased by CHF 12 per month (CHF 144 annually). The optical contribution alone reduced his yearly expenses without changing where he purchased his eyewear.

cases.name: Sophie, 31
cases.body: Sophie enjoys strength training and pays CHF 900 per year for her gym membership. She switched to CSS Livo Top, which includes contributions towards recognised fitness centres and health promotion alongside broader outpatient benefits. Her supplementary premium increased by CHF 15 per month (CHF 180 annually). With an annual contribution towards her eligible fitness membership, she reduced the cost of maintaining an active lifestyle while gaining additional outpatient benefits she previously did not have.
